Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

vignette: Clara Rossi was nine when she learned to read the room for violence. It began in the kitchen of her family home, but what stayed with her was not the shouting itself, but the exact sequence: her father’s belt buckle catching the morning light, the sudden arc of his arm, her mother’s back meeting the wallpapered wall, and the sharp crack of a ceramic pitcher splitting on the linoleum. Clara had been sitting at the small wooden table, knees pulled to her chest, watching. She remembers the table edge pressing into her palms with perfect clarity, but the minutes before and after the outburst slide into a fog. No matter how hard she tries now to reconstruct those lost hours, the gaps remain, as though a curtain had been drawn over them. When the memories surface, her shoulders rise instinctively, her spine curving forward exactly as it did at nine, her palms flattening against an invisible tabletop. Over the years, Clara’s attention fixed on the same cues. She came to believe that harm arrives without warning, and that the only way to endure it is to confine herself to a narrow circle of reliable spaces. She feels secure only within the walls of her home study, behind the heavy door of her car, and at the council chamber podium during scheduled sessions. Anywhere else, she scans the room, her eyes tracking the set of a stranger’s jaw, the quickness of a hand gesture, the shift of weight that might precede a sudden strike. At City Hall, where she now serves as a City Council Member, this vigilance guides her movements. She times her committee appearances to avoid peak hours, sidesteps the narrow corridors near the press gallery, and steps back when colleagues lean over desks, certain that a sudden movement there would echo the kitchen wall. These habits settled over weeks and months, becoming quiet routines. She stopped attending the late receptions in the rotunda, opting instead to slip out early to her car, leaving colleagues to note her quiet departures. Her nights grew restless. Clara lies awake, her body still locked in that childhood posture, waiting for the floor to tremble or the door to latch open. She does not fall asleep until the house settles, and she wakes repeatedly, alert to the creak of the roof or the rumble of a passing truck. Her avoidance exists alongside her professional days. She drafts her speeches in her home study, reviews budget amendments in her car, and rarely stays past four o’clock in the chamber. The missed conversations in the hallway, the late-night calls she lets ring, and the steady withdrawal from after-hours committee gatherings have become a familiar pattern. Her husband notices the careful distance she keeps, the way she watches his hands when he reaches for the remote, the way she measures the space between them. Her PCL-5 score of 54 mirrors a nervous system that holds both precision and pause. Now, at thirty-nine, Clara sits in her council office, the late afternoon light catching the same wooden grain of the table where she once watched. The triggers remain precise: a raised voice, a shifting stance, the sudden snap of a folder. She has come to understand that the world has not changed, only her capacity to read it. What she is most afraid of is the unexpected return of that kitchen floor, the unremembered moments breaking through, the body remembering before the mind catches up, the safe zones shrinking until she has nowhere left to stand. She is seeking help; the late-night restlessness has spilled into her days, and she hopes to learn how to stay in a room without bracing for impact.
